entry.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of John Richardson, Baptised 25 September 1832, Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire

**Conclusion:** The preponderance of evidence from two independent original Lancashire parish registers strongly supports the conclusion that John Richardson—baptised 25 September 1832 at St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire, and later an LDS pioneer who died 10 March 1906 in Richmond, Cache County, Utah—was the son of Thomas Richardson (spinner) and Mary Mallalieu Richardson.

### Primary Evidence: Original Baptism Register

The strongest direct evidence is entry no. 2040 in the original baptism register of St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, read from FHL microfilm 4421674.¹ This is an original source containing primary information, created by J. Hardman, the officiating curate, at the time of the event. The entry reads: "September 25—John—Thomas X Richardson [father], Mary [mother]—Town—Spinner—J. Hardman." Thomas signed with a mark (X). The record places the family in the town of Ashton-under-Lyne and identifies the father's occupation as spinner.

¹ "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org : accessed 22 July 2026), St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, baptism register, pp. 254–255, entry no. 2040, John, son of Thomas Richardson and Mary, 25 September 1832; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm 4421674.

### Independent Corroboration: Original Marriage Register

The marriage register of St Leonard, Walton-le-Dale, records at entry no. 684 that "Thos Richardson, Bachelor of this Parish Chapelry and Mary Mallalieu, Spinster of this Parish Chapelry were married in this Chapel by Banns this Twelfth Day of November in the Year One thousand eight hundred and twenty six By me Henry Fielden Sub Curate." Both parties signed by mark.² This original source, containing primary information created by the officiant at the time of the ceremony, establishes the marriage of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu on 12 November 1826—nearly seven years before John's baptism—and identifies the mother's maiden surname as Mallalieu. Walton-le-Dale is immediately adjacent to Preston, the town recorded as John's birthplace in the family tree, consistent with the family's presence in that part of Lancashire. Thomas's mark-signing at both events is a consistent identifying detail linking the groom of 1826 with the father of 1832.

² "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm.

### Corroborating Derivative Sources

Two derivative FamilySearch index entries—both classified as derivative sources carrying secondary information—corroborate the original records. The first, indexed from FHL microfilm of the same Ashton-under-Lyne register, names the father as Thomas Richardson and the mother as Mary, with a christening date of 25 September 1832.³ The second indexes the Walton-le-Dale marriage of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu on 12 November 1826.⁴ These derivative sources add no facts beyond the originals but confirm the indexing of both registers.

³ "England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9H1K-BYQ : 4 February 2023, Entry for John Richardson, 25 Sep 1832); citing index based upon data collected by the Genealogical Society of Utah, Salt Lake City; FHL microfilm.

⁴ "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QJDD-R1CZ : 9 March 2024), Entry for Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 Nov 1826; St Leonard, Walton le Dale, Lancashire, England; citing FHL microfilm of original parish register.

### Identity of the Subject

John Richardson of the project tree (LR9N-VGQ, died 10 March 1906, Richmond, Cache County, Utah) is identified with the child in entry no. 2040 by the agreement of given name, surname, parish, and date—the same name, the same church at Ashton-under-Lyne, and the same day and month (25 September), with only a one-year discrepancy between the register date of 1832 and the tree's recorded date of 1833. Both the derivative index (ark:/61903/1:1:JMF4-CL9) and the original register agree on 1832; the tree's 1833 date reflects a likely transcription error in a later compilation. This discrepancy does not affect the parentage conclusion, which is consistent across all four sources.

### Conflicts and Limitations

No conflict exists among the sources regarding the parentage. All four sources are mutually consistent: they name Thomas Richardson as the father and Mary (Mallalieu) as the mother of John baptised 25 September at Ashton-under-Lyne. The mother's maiden surname appears only in the marriage register, not in the christening register, but both records are independently consistent, and the marriage register directly supplies the Mallalieu maiden name.

Research is not formally declared exhaustive. English census records beginning in 1841, burial and death records for Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, and baptism records for other children of this couple in the Ashton-under-Lyne or Walton-le-Dale area have not been searched. Those records are expected to corroborate the established parentage rather than alter it.

added.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of John Richardson, Baptised 25 September 1832, Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire

**Conclusion:** The preponderance of evidence from two independent original Lancashire parish registers strongly supports the conclusion that John Richardson—baptised 25 September 1832 at St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, Lancashire, and later an LDS pioneer who died 10 March 1906 in Richmond, Cache County, Utah—was the son of Thomas Richardson (spinner) and Mary Mallalieu Richardson.

### Primary Evidence: Original Baptism Register

The strongest direct evidence is entry no. 2040 in the original baptism register of St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, read from FHL microfilm 4421674.¹ This is an original source containing primary information, created by J. Hardman, the officiating curate, at the time of the event. The entry reads: "September 25—John—Thomas X Richardson [father], Mary [mother]—Town—Spinner—J. Hardman." Thomas signed with a mark (X). The record places the family in the town of Ashton-under-Lyne and identifies the father's occupation as spinner.

¹ "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org : accessed 22 July 2026), St Michael and All Angels, Ashton-under-Lyne, baptism register, pp. 254–255, entry no. 2040, John, son of Thomas Richardson and Mary, 25 September 1832; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm 4421674.

### Independent Corroboration: Original Marriage Register

The marriage register of St Leonard, Walton-le-Dale, records at entry no. 684 that "Thos Richardson, Bachelor of this Parish Chapelry and Mary Mallalieu, Spinster of this Parish Chapelry were married in this Chapel by Banns this Twelfth Day of November in the Year One thousand eight hundred and twenty six By me Henry Fielden Sub Curate." Both parties signed by mark.² This original source, containing primary information created by the officiant at the time of the ceremony, establishes the marriage of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu on 12 November 1826—nearly seven years before John's baptism—and identifies the mother's maiden surname as Mallalieu. Walton-le-Dale is immediately adjacent to Preston, the town recorded as John's birthplace in the family tree, consistent with the family's presence in that part of Lancashire. Thomas's mark-signing at both events is a consistent identifying detail linking the groom of 1826 with the father of 1832.

² "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910," digital image, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:S3HY-6PR3-4VC : accessed 22 July 2026), St Leonard, Walton le Dale, marriage register, p. 228, entry no. 684, Thos Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 November 1826; citing original register held at Lancashire Record Office, Preston; FHL microfilm.

### Corroborating Derivative Sources

Two derivative FamilySearch index entries—both classified as derivative sources carrying secondary information—corroborate the original records. The first, indexed from FHL microfilm of the same Ashton-under-Lyne register, names the father as Thomas Richardson and the mother as Mary, with a christening date of 25 September 1832.³ The second indexes the Walton-le-Dale marriage of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu on 12 November 1826.⁴ These derivative sources add no facts beyond the originals but confirm the indexing of both registers.

³ "England, Births and Christenings, 1538-1975," database, FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:2:9H1K-BYQ : 4 February 2023, Entry for John Richardson, 25 Sep 1832); citing index based upon data collected by the Genealogical Society of Utah, Salt Lake City; FHL microfilm.

⁴ "England, Lancashire, Parish Registers 1538-1910", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QJDD-R1CZ : 9 March 2024), Entry for Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, 12 Nov 1826; St Leonard, Walton le Dale, Lancashire, England; citing FHL microfilm of original parish register.

### Identity of the Subject

John Richardson of the project tree (LR9N-VGQ, died 10 March 1906, Richmond, Cache County, Utah) is identified with the child in entry no. 2040 by the agreement of given name, surname, parish, and date—the same name, the same church at Ashton-under-Lyne, and the same day and month (25 September), with only a one-year discrepancy between the register date of 1832 and the tree's recorded date of 1833. Both the derivative index (ark:/61903/1:1:JMF4-CL9) and the original register agree on 1832; the tree's 1833 date reflects a likely transcription error in a later compilation. This discrepancy does not affect the parentage conclusion, which is consistent across all four sources.

### Conflicts and Limitations

No conflict exists among the sources regarding the parentage. All four sources are mutually consistent: they name Thomas Richardson as the father and Mary (Mallalieu) as the mother of John baptised 25 September at Ashton-under-Lyne. The mother's maiden surname appears only in the marriage register, not in the christening register, but both records are independently consistent, and the marriage register directly supplies the Mallalieu maiden name.

Research is not formally declared exhaustive. English census records beginning in 1841, burial and death records for Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu, and baptism records for other children of this couple in the Ashton-under-Lyne or Walton-le-Dale area have not been searched. Those records are expected to corroborate the established parentage rather than alter it.

### Conclusion and Tier

The evidence strongly supports the conclusion that John Richardson was the son of Thomas Richardson and Mary Mallalieu. Two independent original parish registers—the Ashton-under-Lyne baptism register (entry no. 2040, 25 September 1832) and the Walton-le-Dale marriage register (entry no. 684, 12 November 1826), each created by an officiating clergyman as a contemporary record of the event—agree on this parentage and are corroborated by two derivative indexes. The tier is **probable**: the evidence presents a strong preponderance in favour of this parentage, and the two original sources with primary information satisfy the core evidentiary requirements for a grounded conclusion. The tier does not reach proved because the research is not formally declared exhaustive.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (b. ca. 1845, d. 1908, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)

### Research Question

Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn, born approximately 1845 and deceased 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania?

### Introduction

The record set assembled for this question supports a *probable* conclusion that **Thomas Flynn was the father of Patrick Flynn**. The evidence for paternity rests on three independent original sources spanning six decades, including a direct statement in a death certificate and corroborating household co-enumerations in two federal censuses. The question of Patrick Flynn's mother is addressed separately below and is **not proved**: no record in the assembled set names Patrick's mother, and the sole proposed candidate is tied to him only by a common and widespread surname.

Each source is classified below as original, derivative, or authored; each information item as primary, secondary, or indeterminate; and each piece of evidence as direct, indirect, or negative.

### Evidence for Paternity

**1850 Federal Census.** The 1850 United States census for Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, records an unnamed male child, age 5, birthplace Ireland, in a household headed by Thomas Flynn, age approximately 32, also born in Ireland.[^1] The 1850 population schedule did not record given names for children under ten or the relationship of household members to the head. The child's sex, stated age, and Irish birthplace are consistent with Patrick Flynn, who in later records reported a birth year of approximately 1845 and a birthplace of Ireland. The household position of the child, immediately following Thomas Flynn and an adult woman, is structurally consistent with a parent-child relationship, but the census does not state one. This source is classified as **original** (enumerated contemporaneously with the events of daily residence), carrying **indeterminate information** (the informant is an unidentified household member, likely Thomas Flynn himself, but the 1850 schedule does not identify the reporting party), and furnishing **indirect evidence** of the parent-child relationship (the relationship is inferred from household position and shared surname, not read from an explicit field).

**1860 Federal Census.** Ten years later, the 1860 federal census for Schuylkill County records Patrick Flynn, age 15, birthplace Ireland, in the household of Thomas Flynn, head, at dwelling 112, family 119.[^2] Patrick's given name appears explicitly in the 1860 schedule. His stated age (15) is consistent with a birth circa 1845, confirming continuity with the child enumerated in Thomas Flynn's household in 1850, and his recorded birthplace (Ireland) matches. The relationship column was not introduced to the federal census until 1880; the parent-child relationship is again inferred from household position, shared surname, and compatible ages. This source is classified as **original**, carrying **indeterminate information** (the informant for the 1860 household is unknown, likely a household member), and furnishing **indirect evidence** of the parent-child relationship.

**1908 Pennsylvania Death Certificate.** Patrick Flynn's death certificate, no. 4521, issued by the Pennsylvania Department of Health, directly names his father as **Thomas Flynn**.[^3] The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. A son-in-law reporting on his father-in-law's parents is a family member not present at the relevant events; he reports from second-hand knowledge, not personal witness. This informant is therefore classified as **secondary** for birth and parentage facts. The record itself is **original** (issued by a state agency from contemporaneous registration), and the parentage entry constitutes **direct evidence** — it answers the parentage question by explicit statement rather than inference. Despite the secondary character of the informant, a direct statement by a family member who knew Patrick personally and had reason to know his father's name carries meaningful weight, particularly when corroborated by two independent census records.

### Assessment of the Paternity Claim

Three independent original sources converge on Thomas Flynn as Patrick Flynn's father. Their informants are distinct — an unknown 1850 household reporter, an unknown 1860 household reporter, and James Brown in 1908 — ruling out the possibility that a single erroneous informant propagated a false claim across all three records. The evidence is genuinely convergent across independent lines, not merely corroborative repetition of one source.

The two census records furnish indirect evidence through household co-enumeration; the death certificate furnishes direct evidence through explicit naming of the father. Together they satisfy GPS Components 2 (complete citations), 3 (analysis and correlation), and 4 (no unresolved conflicts bearing on paternity — the birthplace conflict is resolved, as discussed below). Component 1 (reasonably exhaustive research) is not fully met: Schuylkill County probate records for Thomas Flynn, church records for the Flynn family, and Irish origin records have not been searched. These record types could corroborate this conclusion, and in an adverse case could complicate it. Because they remain unsearched, research is not declared exhaustive, and the conclusion is accordingly **probable** rather than proved.

### Evidence Bearing on Maternity

The sole evidence proposed in support of a maternal connection is the 1870 federal census entry for a woman named Bridget Flynn, age 52, enumerated as a widow and head of household in Schuylkill County.[^4] No children appear in her 1870 household, which is consistent with Patrick being approximately 25 and already living independently by that year. The 1870 census search that returned this entry found three other Flynn households in the county, none of which could be clearly tied to Thomas Flynn's known household from the 1850 and 1860 census records.

This source is classified as **original**, carrying **indeterminate information** (the informant is unknown, most likely Bridget Flynn herself reporting to the enumerator), and furnishing evidence that is **indirect at best** for a maternal connection to Patrick Flynn. The reasoning chain underlying hypothesis h_002 is: (1) Patrick's father was Thomas Flynn; (2) Bridget Flynn is a widow named Flynn in the same county in 1870; therefore (3) Bridget might be Thomas Flynn's widow and Patrick's mother. Every step is problematic. Step 1 is concluded at probable, not proved. Step 2 establishes only that a woman named Bridget Flynn was widowed in Schuylkill County in 1870 — it does not name her late husband, does not connect her to the Thomas Flynn household known from 1850 and 1860, and provides no identifying detail that distinguishes this Bridget from any other Flynn widow the county might contain. "Flynn" is a common surname in Schuylkill County. The coincidence of surname and widowhood is not, by itself, evidence of familial connection.

No record in the assembled set names Patrick Flynn's mother. No marriage record for Thomas Flynn was located. No death record for Thomas Flynn was found that might name a surviving widow. The person-evidence link for Bridget Flynn was assigned a match score of 0.0002 and a confidence rating of speculative — a near-zero score reflecting the weakness just described. The proposed maternal connection remains at hypothesis stage (h_002, status: active), explicitly distinguished from the supported paternity hypothesis, with project notes warning that it rests on a common surname and nothing more.

Records that could establish or refute this claim — Thomas Flynn's estate file if one was opened in Schuylkill County probate, church records naming Thomas Flynn's wife in a marriage, baptism, or burial entry, and any Irish origin records — have not been searched. The maternal parentage of Patrick Flynn is therefore **not proved**.

### Resolved Conflict

A conflict arose between the birthplace recorded for Patrick Flynn in the 1850 and 1860 census entries (Ireland) and the birthplace on the 1908 death certificate (Pennsylvania).[^5] This conflict (c_001) has been resolved in favor of Ireland: the two census records are contemporaneous original sources, with informants who were household members likely to have first-hand knowledge of where Patrick was born; the death certificate informant, James Brown (son-in-law), was secondary for birth facts and may have confused Patrick's long-time Pennsylvania residence with his actual birthplace. The resolved birthplace conflict does not affect the paternity conclusion.

### Conclusion

The preponderance of evidence establishes, with **probable confidence**, that **Thomas Flynn was the father of Patrick Flynn** of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Three independent original sources — the 1850 federal census, the 1860 federal census, and the 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate — consistently indicate this relationship; the death certificate states it directly, and the two censuses corroborate it through household co-enumeration spanning a decade. No evidence contradicts this conclusion.

The **maternal parentage of Patrick Flynn is not proved**. The sole proposed candidate, Bridget Flynn, widow, Schuylkill County, 1870 census, is connected to Patrick Flynn and Thomas Flynn only by a common and widespread surname. Church records, probate records, and Irish origin records that could name Patrick's mother or Thomas Flynn's wife have not been searched.

---

[^1]: 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.

[^2]: 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.

[^3]: Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

[^4]: 1870 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, Bridget Flynn (widow) household; NARA microfilm publication M593, roll 1355; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 4 May 2026.

[^5]: The birthplace conflict (c_001) is addressed by the same three sources cited above: citations at [^1], [^2], and [^3].

## Who Was the Mother of Cornelis van Noord (b. ~1828, Zuid-Holland)?

### The Research Question

Both surviving records that name the mother of Cornelis van Noord agree that she was his mother and that her surname was van Noord. They disagree on the first letter of her given name. After exhausting every record type that could resolve the conflict, no independent witness survives to cast a deciding vote.

### Evidence

**Birth act of 1828 (original record, primary information, father as informant)**

The 1828 civil birth register of Zuid-Holland, birth act no. 42, records the birth of Cornelis van Noord and names his mother as "Jannetje [?] van Noord."[^1] The father of Cornelis appeared as the declarant before the municipal registrar, making him the informant for his wife's name — a household member with direct personal knowledge. The source is an original civil register; the information is primary; and the record basis is a contemporaneous stated declaration. However, a material difficulty prevents full reliance on this reading: the initial letter of the mother's given name is unreadable in the handwritten act. The FamilySearch OCR transcription reads the letter as "J"; the researcher who examined the same image independently read it as "T." Both readings are paleographically plausible; neither is certain.

**Ten-year marriage index, 1843–1852 (derivative record, secondary information, clerk as informant)**

The Tienjarige tafels (ten-year marriage index) of Zuid-Holland, 1843–1852, names the mother of Cornelis van Noord as "Fannetje van Noord."[^2] This index is a derivative abstract compiled by a municipal clerk from one or more underlying marriage acts. The clerk acted in an official capacity but had no personal knowledge of the family; the information is accordingly secondary. The index is legible at the first letter ("F"), but, being a derivative record, it reflects the clerk's reading of a source that is not itself on file.

### Conflict c_001: Three Readings, One Letter

The three candidate readings — "Jannetje," "Tannetje," and "Fannetje" — are each consistent with the remaining letters "-annetje." The birth act is the original, contemporaneous record and ordinarily carries the greater evidentiary weight, but its first letter is physically unreadable at precisely the character in dispute, which nullifies that advantage here. The index is legible at the disputed point but derivative and compiled years after the birth. Neither source outweighs the other for this specific character; no preference can be assigned. The birth act and the marriage index are independent of each other, but the researcher's reading of the birth-act image is a third interpretation of the same entry as the OCR, not an independent witness.

### Elimination of Alternative Records

Every record type that might independently name this woman has been searched:

- **Duplicate of the 1828 birth register**: Does not survive.
- **Marriage act for Cornelis van Noord** (which would repeat the mother's name): Lost in both register copies; the marriage supplements do not survive.
- **Death act for the mother**: Not found.
- **Death act for Cornelis**: Not found.
- **Death act for the husband**: Found, but it blots the mother's given name at the same initial letter as the birth act — providing no resolution.
- **Population-register entry**: None survives for this family.
- **Birth acts for siblings**: Not found.
- **Parents' marriage act**: Not found.

No reachable record remains that could supply the mother's given name from an independent source.

### Conclusion

The evidence establishes that the mother of Cornelis van Noord was a woman surnamed van Noord — confirmed by both records — whose given name contained the string "-annetje" and began with a letter that is unreadable in the original act and variably recorded in the derivative index. Her identity as the mother is not in dispute; what cannot be concluded is the precise given name. The conflict over the first letter of that name is material to a complete answer to the research question and has resisted every available avenue of resolution. The conclusion is assessed as **possible**: the broad outline of the mother's identity is established, but an irresolvable ambiguity prevents a firmer statement of who she was by name.

Conflict c_001 remains open. Re-running conflict-resolution would weigh the same evidence against the same exhausted record landscape and could not yield a different result.

[^1]: Burgerlijke Stand, Zuid-Holland, Netherlands, birth act no. 42, 1828, Cornelis van Noord.
[^2]: Tienjarige tafels (ten-year marriage index), Zuid-Holland, Netherlands, 1843-1852, Cornelis van Noord.

entry.narrative_markdown:
## Patrick Flynn — Parents: Not Proved

**Research Question:** Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (born approximately 1845 in Ireland; resident Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania)?

**Conclusion:** The parentage of Patrick Flynn cannot be established. This question was closed under a researcher wrap-up directive before any records were searched or analyzed. No assertions, sources, or person-evidence entries exist in the project record. The conclusion is therefore *not proved* solely because the research was not conducted, not because the evidence is unavailing.

**What Would Be Required**

Establishing Patrick Flynn's parentage would call for searches in at least the following record classes:

1. **U.S. federal census records, 1850–1880, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.** These are the logical first step. The 1880 schedule names parents' birthplaces and relationship to head; the 1860 and 1870 schedules may capture siblings or parents in the same household. An 1850 entry could place Patrick in a parental household while still a minor.

2. **Passenger arrival lists and naturalization papers.** Irish emigrants to the Pennsylvania coal regions often arrived in the 1840s–1860s. Naturalization declarations sometimes name county of origin in Ireland; pre-1906 passenger lists may carry that detail as well.

3. **Pennsylvania church records, Schuylkill County.** Catholic parishes serving the Irish mining communities (Pottsville, Minersville, Mahanoy City) kept baptismal and marriage registers. A marriage record for Patrick Flynn would typically name his father, and sometimes his mother.

4. **Pennsylvania death certificate (post-1906).** If Patrick Flynn died in Pennsylvania after statewide death registration began in 1906, his death certificate may name his parents. Pennsylvania did not register deaths statewide before that year.

5. **Irish records.** Once a county or parish of origin is identified, Irish civil birth registers (from 1864), Catholic parish registers, Griffith's Valuation (1847–1864), and Tithe Applotment Books could document a Flynn family. Without a place of origin, Irish record searches are impractical.

**Tier: Not Proved.** No evidence was gathered. The shortfall is a research gap, not an exhausted record set: every record class listed above is reachable, and the question should be reopened if research resumes.
